questions.q: Per this lesson, why can a technically perfect deployment still fail as a release?
options: Technical success always guarantees organizational success automatically

If end users don't know a capability exists, don't understand why something changed, or work around a new process because nobody explained it, the release fails in the way that actually matters to the business
Because Salesforce requires every deployment to be manually re-approved after go-live
Because technical deployments are never actually successful on Salesforce
questions.explain: The lesson's central point is that passing every technical gate doesn't guarantee organizational success -- that requires users to actually understand and adopt the change, which is what release communication and training exist to ensure.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say support and help desk staff need to be briefed before end users?
options: Support staff never need to know about releases at all
End users are legally required to be notified after support staff in every case
Support staff are responsible for approving every release before it ships
Being blindsided by a change their own users already know about, while support doesn't, quickly damages credibility for the whole release process
questions.explain: If end users already know about a change and start calling with questions before support has been briefed, support looks unprepared -- which is why briefing them ahead of end users matters.

questions.q: How does this lesson describe the right approach to Salesforce's own seasonal release notes?
options: Forward the entire release notes document to every end user unfiltered
Ignore seasonal release notes entirely, since they only affect Salesforce's own infrastructure

Review the notes for the small subset that actually affects this org's own users, and translate just that relevant slice into the same plain-language, audience-specific communication used for internal changes
Only executives need to see Salesforce's seasonal release notes
questions.explain: The skill described is filtering: most of a seasonal release's content is irrelevant to any one org, so the practice is identifying and translating only the relevant subset for the org's actual users.

questions.q: What is adoption tracking, as defined in this lesson?
options: Checking after go-live whether users are actually using a new feature or following a new process, rather than reverting to an old workaround
A Salesforce feature that automatically trains new users
A step in the change-control approval process that happens before deployment
The process of refreshing a sandbox on schedule
questions.explain: Adoption tracking happens after go-live and closes the loop on whether communication and training actually worked, by checking real usage rather than assuming the announcement was enough.

questions.q: If a month after go-live almost no sales reps are correctly filling in a new mandatory field, what does this lesson say that most likely signals?
options: A pure technical failure in the field's configuration, unrelated to communication
That the field should never have been made mandatory under any circumstances
That the communication or training didn't land as intended, which should feed back into how the next release's communication plan is built
That the CAB failed to approve the change correctly
questions.explain: The lesson frames low adoption of a working feature as a communication/training signal, not necessarily a technical defect -- and says that signal should inform future release communication planning.
